newsitem.title: USA: Currency market volatility undesirable, Rubin says.
newsitem.headline: Currency market volatility undesirable, Rubin says.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Thursday called excessive currency market volatility "undesirable" but said he was unsure if the dollar's recent gyrations qualified for that description.
"I don't know if it represents excessive volatility, but I do think excessive volatility is undesirable," he told reporters following a speech here.

He added that he expects the Group of Seven finance ministers to discuss recent currency volatility when they meet next week in Denver under the rubric of the annual summit meeting of their nations' leaders.
"At the finance ministers' meeting, I don't know about the leaders, I suspect we'll discuss recent volatility in the market," Rubin said.
The Treasury chief said that U.S. dollar policy remains unchanged and that Washington is committed to not using its currency as a trade tool.
"We have never used and will not use our currency as an instrument of trade policy," Rubin said.

Rubin though did reiterate his opposition to a sustained, significant rise in Japan's trade surplus. "We think a sustained increase in the surplus -- sustained -- could hurt global growth ... and has the potential at least for creating a protectionist backlash," he said.

Asked if the surplus has already been rising on a sustained basis, Rubin said, "I think we all have to watch and see what happens. I certainly don't think one would be influenced by a month or quarter."
Japan's current account surplus jumped by more than 90 percent in April from a year earlier.
Rubin said Japan's trade surplus was not on the agenda of next week's G7 summit in Denver, but he added that it could come up when finance ministers meet there.

"It is not on the agenda as such," he said. "I can't speak for the leaders' meetings, but at least when finance ministers get together, you touch on all kinds of things that are involved in the world economy, so it could come up."
He made clear he remaine upbeat on the outlook for the U.S. economy, despite the drop in retail sales over the past three months.
"The economy remains in good shape," he said. "Far and away the most likely outlook looking forward is contionuation of favorable conditions, both for growth and inflation."
